{{Short description|British epidemiologist (1807–1883)}}
{{other people}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=August 2021}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2012}}
[[File:PSM V23 D302 William Farr.jpg|thumb|William Farr]]
'''William Farr''' [[Order of the Bath|CB]] (30 November 1807 – 14 April 1883) was a British [[epidemiologist]], regarded as one of the founders of [[medical statistics]].

==Early life==
William Farr was born in [[Kenley, Shropshire]], to poor parents.  He was effectively adopted by a local squire, Joseph Pryce, when Farr and his family moved to [[Dorrington, Shropshire|Dorrington]]. In 1826 he took a job as a dresser (surgeon's assistant) in the [[Royal Salop Infirmary|Salop Infirmary]] in [[Shrewsbury, Shropshire|Shrewsbury]] and served a nominal apprenticeship to an [[apothecary]]. Pryce died in November 1828, and left Farr £500 ({{Inflation|UK|500|1828|r=-2|fmt=eq|cursign=£}}), which allowed him to study medicine in [[France]] and [[Switzerland]].<ref name="ODNB"/> In Paris he heard [[Pierre Charles Alexandre Louis]] lecture.<ref>{{cite book|author=Ian Hacking|title=The Taming of Chance|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780521388849|url-access=registration|access-date=21 June 2013|date=31 August 1990|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-38884-9|page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780521388849/page/84 84]}}</ref>

Farr returned to England in 1831 and continued his studies at [[University College London]], qualifying as a licentiate of the [[Society of Apothecaries]] in March 1832. He married in 1833 and started a medical practice in [[Fitzroy Square]], London.  He became involved in medical journalism and statistics.<ref name="ODNB"/>

==General Register Office==
[[File:William Farr 2.jpg|thumb|William Farr, about 1850]]
In 1837 the [[General Register Office for England and Wales|General Register Office]] (GRO) took on the responsibility for the [[United Kingdom Census 1841]]. Farr was hired there, initially on a temporary basis to handle data from [[vital registration]].<ref name="ODNB">{{cite ODNB|id=9185|title=Farr, William|first=John M.|last=Eyler}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=William G. Rothstein|title=Public Health and the Risk Factor: A History of an Uneven Medical Revolution|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rmwp7X2FZ68C&pg=PA29|access-date=21 June 2013|year=2003|publisher=Boydell & Brewer|isbn=978-1-58046-127-6|page=29}}</ref> Then, with a recommendation from [[Edwin Chadwick]] and backing from [[Neil Arnott]], Farr secured another post in the GRO as the first compiler of scientific abstracts (i.e. a statistician).<ref>{{cite book|author=Dorothy Porter|title=Health, Civilization, and the State: A History of Public Health from Ancient to Modern Times|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XswTsHJbQf8C&pg=PA70|access-date=21 June 2013|year=1999|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-20036-3|page=70}}</ref><ref>{{cite ODNB|id=694|title=Arnott, Neil|first=Bill|last=Luckin}}</ref> Chadwick and Farr had an agenda, demography aimed at [[public health]], and the support of the initial Registrar General [[Thomas Henry Lister]]. Lister worked with Farr on the census design, to forward the programme.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Raymond Flood|author-link=Raymond Flood (mathematician)|author2=Adrian Rice|author3=Robin Wilson|author3-link=Robin Wilson (mathematician)|title=Mathematics in Victorian Britain|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QmzfJUShGYUC&pg=PA269|access-date=21 June 2013|date=29 September 2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-960139-4|page=269}}</ref>

Farr was responsible for the collection of official medical statistics in England and Wales.  His most important contribution was to set up a system for routinely recording the causes of death.  For example, for the first time it allowed the [[mortality rate]]s of different occupations to be compared.

==Learned societies and associations==
In 1839, Farr joined the [[Royal Statistical Society|Statistical Society]], in which he played an active part as treasurer, vice-president and president over the years. In 1855 he was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=Norman L. Johnson|author2=Samuel Kotz|title=Leading Personalities in Statistical Sciences: From the Seventeenth Century to the Present|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AzZZ-uW6WuEC&pg=PA286|access-date=22 June 2013|date=26 September 2011|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-15072-6|pages=286}}</ref> He was involved in the [[National Association for the Promotion of Social Science|Social Science Association]] from its foundation in 1857,<ref>{{cite book|author=Lawrence Goldman|title=Science, Reform, and Politics in Victorian Britain|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=io2nB6RcaIwC&pg=PA174|access-date=22 June 2013|year=2002|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-43301-3|page=174}}</ref> taking part in its Quarantine Committee and Committee on Trades' Societies and Strikes.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Michael J. Lacey|author2=Mary O. Furner|title=The State and Social Investigation in Britain and the United States|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xOKwKZNzbQ0C&pg=PA107|access-date=22 June 2013|date=25 June 1993|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-41638-2|page=107}}</ref>

== Law of epidemics ==
{{main article|Farr's laws}}
In 1840, Farr submitted a letter to the ''Annual Report of the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages in England''.  In that letter, he applied mathematics to the records of deaths during a recent [[smallpox]] epidemic, proposing that:

<blockquote>"If the latent cause of epidemics cannot be discovered, the mode in which it operates may be investigated.  The laws of its action may be determined by observation, as well as the circumstances in which epidemics arise, or by which they may be controlled."<ref>(Farr, 1840), p. 95.</ref></blockquote>

He showed that during the smallpox epidemic, a plot of the number of deaths per quarter followed a roughly bell-shaped or "[[normal distribution|normal curve]]",<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Farr |first1=William |title=Causes of death in England and Wales |journal=Second Annual Report of the Registrar General of Births, Deaths and Marriages in England |date=1840 |volume=2 |pages=69–98 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101064041955&view=1up&seq=71}} On p. 97, Farr stated that during a recent smallpox epidemic, the number of deaths versus time followed a roughly normal curve:  "The rates vary with the density of the population, the numbers susceptible of attack, the mortality, and the accidental circumstances; so that to obtain the mean rates applicable to the whole population, or to any portion of the population, several epidemics should be investigated.  It appears probable, however, that the small-pox increases at an accelerated and then a retarded rate; that it declines first at a slightly accelerated, and at a rapidly accelerated, and lastly at a retarded rate, until the disease attains the minimum intensity, and remains stationary."</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brownlee |first1=John |title=Historical note on Farr's theory of the epidemic |journal=The British Medical Journal, Part 2 |date=1915 |volume=2 |issue=2850 |pages=250–252 |doi=10.1136/bmj.2.2850.250 |pmid=20767766 |pmc=2302838 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=iau.31858012721373&view=1up&seq=298&size=125}}  From p. 250:  "He specially considered the decline of the [smallpox] epidemic, and fitted the figures to a curve calculated by a method described.  Though he gives no equation of the form of the curve, it is quite obviously the normal curve of error."</ref> and that recent epidemics of other diseases had followed a similar pattern.<ref>(Farr, 1840), p. 98. "Table (q) exhibits the progress of four more epidemic diseases in the metropolis, – measles, typhus, hooping-cough, and scarlatina, – which have not yet been effectively controlled by medical science.  They exhibit the same regularity, but the laws which govern their course will be more conveniently discussed when the abstract of the observations has been extended over another year."</ref>

==Research on cholera==
There was a major outbreak of [[cholera]] in London in 1849 which killed around 15,000 people.  Early industrialisation had made London the most populous city in the world at the time, and the [[River Thames]] was heavily polluted with untreated sewage. Farr subscribed to the conventional theory that cholera was carried by polluted air rather than water – the [[miasma theory of disease|miasmic theory]]. In addition, through his analysis of several variables and their association with death from cholera, Farr held the belief that elevation was the major contributor to the occurrence of the disease.<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Bingham
| first1 = P.
| last2 = Verlander
| first2 = N. Q.
| last3 = Cheal
| first3 = M. J.
| date = 2004-09-01
| title = John Snow, William Farr and the 1849 outbreak of cholera that affected London: a reworking of the data highlights the importance of the water supply
| journal = Public Health
| volume = 118
| issue = 6
| pages = 387–394
| doi = 10.1016/j.puhe.2004.05.007
| issn = 0033-3506
| pmid = 15313591
}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Johnson |first=Steven |authorlink=Steven Johnson (author) |title=Extra Life |publisher=[[Riverhead Books]] |year=2021 |isbn=978-0-525-53885-1 |edition=1st |pages=80-81 |language=en}}</ref> He also presented how topographical features are able to prevent certain diseases similarly to immunization.<ref>{{Cite web
| url = http://brianaltonenmph.com/gis/historical-medical-geography/1852-william-farr-elevation-and-cholera/
| title = 1852 – William Farr's Elevation and Cholera paper
| website = Brian Altonen, MPH, MS
| date = 7 December 2012
| language = en-US
| access-date = 2016-02-25
}}</ref>

During the 1853-54 epidemic, Farr gathered more statistical evidence.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Eyler|first=J. M.|date=2001|title=The changing assessments of John Snow's and William Farr's cholera studies|url=http://www.epidemiology.ch/history/papers/eyler-paper-1.pdf|journal=Sozial- und Präventivmedizin|volume=46|issue=4|pages=225–232|issn=0303-8408|pmid=11582849|doi=10.1007/bf01593177|s2cid=9549345}}</ref> During focused study of the [[1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak]], the physician [[John Snow (physician)|John Snow]] used data supplied by the GRO<ref>{{cite book |last=Snow |first=John |date= 1855 |title= On the Mode of Communication of Cholera. 2nd ed| location= London |publisher= John Churchill |url= http://archive.org/details/b28985266. | page=39}}</ref> and applied the (now accepted) mechanism for transmission he had proposed in 1849:<ref>Snow, John. 1849. On the Mode of Communication of Cholera. London: John Churchill.</ref> people were infected by swallowing something, and it multiplied in the [[intestine]]s.  Snow also examined mortality statistics compiled by the GRO for people supplied with water from two companies in South London – the [[Southwark and Vauxhall Waterworks Company]] (which drew contaminated water from low in the Thames basin) and the [[Lambeth Waterworks Company]] (which drew cleaner water from further up the Thames) – and found Southwark and Vauxhall customers were especially likely to suffer.<ref>Aschengrau, A. & Seage, G. R. (2008). Essentials of epidemiology in public health. Pg:15-21 Sudbury, Mass.: Jones And Bartlett Publishers.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Snow |first=John |date= 1855 |title= On the Mode of Communication of Cholera. 2nd ed| location= London |publisher= John Churchill |url= http://archive.org/details/b28985266. | pages=86, 89}}</ref>

Farr took part in the [[General Board of Health]]'s 1854 Committee for Scientific Enquiries. The conventional explanation for cholera was still [[contingent contagionism|multifactorial]]; Snow's view of cholera as solely caused by a [[pathogen]] was not accepted, though his evidence was taken seriously. Farr's research was detailed and showed an inverse correlation of mortality and elevation.<ref>{{cite book|author=Alfredo Morabia|title=A History of Epidemiologic Methods and Concepts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E-OZbEmPSTkC&pg=PA133|access-date=22 June 2013|date=1 January 2004|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-7643-6818-0|pages=133–4}}</ref>

There was a further epidemic in 1866, by which time Snow had died, and Farr had accepted Snow's explanation. He produced a monograph which showed that mortality was extremely high for people who drew their water from the Old Ford Reservoir in East London. Farr's work was then considered conclusive.

==Later life==
In 1858, he performed a study on the correlation of health and marriage condition, and found that health decreases from the married to the unmarried to the widowed.<ref>Tara Parker-Pope (14 April 2010). [https://www.nytimes.com/2010/04/18/magazine/18marriage-t.html Is Marriage Good for Your Health?] New York Times</ref> In the period 1857–9 the Office ordered a [[difference engine]], a model designed by Swedish followers of [[Charles Babbage]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Michael Lindgren|title=Glory and Failure: The Difference Engines of Johann Müller, Charles Babbage and Georg and Edvard Scheutz|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=plgMl2yfVkwC&pg=PA289|access-date=21 June 2013|year=1990|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=978-0-262-12146-0|page=289}}</ref> The intended application was the "British Life Table".<ref>{{cite book|author=Jeremy M. Norman|title=From Gutenberg to the Internet: A Sourcebook on the History of Information Technology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=emmitTbOoFgC&pg=PA134|access-date=21 June 2013|date=1 January 2005|publisher=Norman Publishing|isbn=978-0-930405-87-8|page=134}}</ref>
[[File:William Farr.jpg|thumb|left|William Farr, about 1870]]

In 1862 Farr was paid £300 ({{Inflation|UK|300|1862|r=-2|fmt=eq|cursign=£}}) for producing a report on the [[Metropolitan Police]] Superannuation Fund, an early pension provision for that organisation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C4732596|title=Home Office: Registered Papers, c1841-1855, 1856-1871 - POLICE (METROPOLITAN): Superannuation Fund: Dr Farr's report; he received £300 from police fund (HO 45/7374)|publisher=[[The National Archives]]}}</ref> He also served as a commissioner in the 1871 census, retiring from the General Register Office in 1879 after he was not given the post of [[Registrar General]], the position going to Sir Brydges Henniker.<ref name="EB1911">{{Cite EB1911|wstitle=Farr, William||volume=10|page=187}}</ref> The same year, Farr received as honours a [[Order of the Bath|Companionship of the Bath]] and the Gold Medal of the [[British Medical Association]] for his work in the field of [[biostatistics]].<ref name="ODNB"/>

In his last years, Farr's approach had become obsolescent. [[Bacteriology]] had changed the face of the medical issues, and statistics became an increasingly mathematic tool. Medical reformers, too, changed approach, expecting less from legislation and central government.<ref>{{cite book|author=Lawrence Goldman|title=Science, Reform, and Politics in Victorian Britain|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=io2nB6RcaIwC&pg=PA200|access-date=23 June 2013|year=2002|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-43301-3|page=200}}</ref>

Farr died aged 75 at his home in [[Maida Vale]], London, and was buried in the churchyard at  Holy Trinity, [[Bromley Common]].<ref name="ODNB"/>

==Works==
In 1837 Farr wrote the chapter "Vital Statistics" for [[John Ramsey McCulloch]]'s ''Statistical Account of the British Empire''. In January 1837 he established the ''[[British Annals of Medicine, Pharmacy, Vital Statistics, and General Science]]'', discontinued in August of that year. He revised a book of [[James Fernandez Clarke]] on [[tuberculosis]].<ref>{{cite book|author1=Norman L. Johnson|author2=Samuel Kotz|title=Leading Personalities in Statistical Sciences: From the Seventeenth Century to the Present|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AzZZ-uW6WuEC&pg=PA284|access-date=22 June 2013|date=26 September 2011|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-15072-6|pages=284}}</ref>

Farr exploited his GRO post compiling abstracts in a way that went beyond the original job description. In so doing he applied the techniques of the English [[actuary]] [[Benjamin Gompertz]] (the [[Gompertz curve]]), and the closely allied statistical "law of mortality" of his fellow actuary [[Thomas Rowe Edmonds]]. Farr, by relying on the existing mathematical model of mortality, could use [[data sampling]] to cut back the required computation.<ref>{{cite book|author=Alfredo Morabia|title=A History of Epidemiologic Methods and Concepts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E-OZbEmPSTkC&pg=PA155|access-date=21 June 2013|date=1 January 2004|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-3-7643-6818-0|page=155}}</ref> From the GRO data he constructed a series of national [[life tables]].<ref name="Stone1997">{{cite book|author=Richard Stone|title=Some British Empiricists in the Social Sciences, 1650-1900|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ccQFbSfF7PIC&pg=PA263|access-date=21 June 2013|year=1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-57145-6|page=263}}</ref>

The theory of [[zymotic disease]] was Farr's contribution to the debate on [[aetiology]]. He identified urbanisation and [[population density]] as public health issues.<ref>{{cite book|author=Thomas Edward Jordan|title=The Degeneracy Crisis and Victorian Youth|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LLNxB-a3n3YC&pg=PA218|access-date=23 June 2013|year=1993|publisher=SUNY Press|isbn=978-1-4384-0804-0|pages=217–8}}</ref> In terms of [[nosology]] he classed epidemic, endemic and contagious diseases as "zymotic", seen as diseases of filth and overcrowding.<ref>{{cite book|author=John M. Eyler|title=Sir Arthur Newsholme and State Medicine, 1885-1935|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9vOcq_BX25YC&pg=PA34|access-date=23 June 2013|date=15 August 2002|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-52458-2|page=34}}</ref>

A selection of his statistical writings was published in 1885, edited by Noël Humphreys.<ref name="EB1911"/>

==In drama==
In "[[Seven Wonders of the Industrial World#The Sewer King|The Sewer King]]", an episode in the 2003 British television documentary series ''[[Seven Wonders of the Industrial World]]'', Farr was played by [[Norman Lovett]].<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0698582/ ''Seven Wonders of the Industrial World'' 'The Sewer King' (2003)]. [[Internet Movie Database]]</ref>

==Family==
Farr's first wife, whom he married in 1833, had the surname Langford; she died of [[tuberculosis]] in 1837.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Dr William Farr of Shropshire (1807–1883): obstetric mortality and training|first=P. M.|last=Dunn|date=1 July 2002|journal=Archives of Disease in Childhood: Fetal and Neonatal Edition|volume=87|issue=1|pages=F67–F69|doi=10.1136/fn.87.1.F67|pmid=12091298|pmc=1721433|doi-access=free}}</ref> He married Mary Elizabeth Whittal in 1842, and they had eight children. In 1880 a public testimonial was collected to provide for his daughters after he lost money through unwise investments.<ref name="ODNB"/> 
[[File:William Farr's name on the Frieze of the LSHTM building .jpg|alt=William Farr's name on the Frieze of the LSHTM building|thumb|William Farr's name on the Frieze of the [[London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine|LSHTM]] building ]]
One daughter, Henrietta, was married to painter and illustrator [[Henry Marriott Paget]], the older brother of illustrators [[Sidney Paget|Sidney]] and [[Walter Paget]]. Another daughter, [[Florence Farr]], was also a painter and artist and a model of many famous [[art deco]] works of art. The Pagets as well as the Farr sisters lived and worked in [[Bedford Park, London|Bedford Park]], the famous artist's colony in West London.

== Recognition ==
Farr's name features on the Frieze of the [[London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine]]. Twenty-three names of public health and tropical medicine pioneers were chosen to appear on the School building in Keppel Street when it was constructed in 1926.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lshtm.ac.uk/library/archives/history/frieze/index.html|title=Behind the Frieze|website=LSHTM|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222110315/http://www.lshtm.ac.uk/library/archives/history/frieze/index.html|archive-date=22 February 2017|url-status=dead|access-date=21 February 2017}}</ref>

In 1884, ''[[Farriolla]]'', which is a [[genus]] of [[fungi]] in the [[Ascomycota]] phylum, was named in William Farr's honour.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Lumbsch TH, Huhndorf SM. |date=December 2007 |title=Outline of Ascomycota &ndash; 2007 |journal=Myconet |volume=13 |pages=1&ndash;58 |url=http://archive.fieldmuseum.org/myconet/outline.asp |publisher=The Field Museum, Department of Botany |location=Chicago, USA |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318003134/http://www.fieldmuseum.org/myconet/outline.asp |archive-date=2009-03-18 }}</ref>
